items.prompt: Black to move. Tap every square the black king can move to.

claims.statement: The black king has exactly these squares.

hints: The king can step to any of the eight squares around it, unless the queen or the white king attacks it.
The queen attacks along ranks, files and diagonals. Which of the eight squares does she cover from c4?
She covers all the squares on the fourth rank, on the c-file, and on two diagonals.
items.explain: From c4 the queen covers d4, e4 and f4 along the fourth rank and d5 and e6 along a diagonal, so only d6, f5 and f6 are open. A queen a knight's jump from the king takes away five of its eight squares.

items.prompt: Black to move. The queen is far away on a8. Tap every square the black king can move to.

claims.statement: The black king has exactly these squares.

hints: Which squares does a queen on a8 attack? Think of its diagonal and the eighth rank.
The diagonal a8-h1 passes through d5 and e4.
items.explain: From a8 the queen only covers d5 and e4 among the squares next to the king, so six squares stay open. The same queen, placed a knight's jump away, would leave only three.

items.prompt: White to move. Find checkmate in one. Careful: two of the strong-looking queen moves are stalemate.
hints: Black's king is in the corner. Which squares does your king already cover?
A move that takes away the last square without giving check is stalemate. You need a check.
Give check along the back rank.
items.explain: Qd8 gives check along the eighth rank and the white king covers a7 and b7: checkmate. Qd6 and Qg3 leave Black without a move but not in check, which is stalemate: only a draw.

feedback_by_move.d3d6: Black has no legal move and is not in check: stalemate, a draw.
feedback_by_move.d3g3: Black has no legal move and is not in check: stalemate, a draw.

items.prompt: White to move. Find a quiet queen move (no check) that forces checkmate on the next move.
hints: Black's king is on the eighth rank. Which squares can it still use?
Your king covers d7, e7 and c7. A queen can take away a whole file.
Put the queen on the f-file, far from the king.
items.explain: Each of these queen moves takes the f-file away from the black king without giving check. It then has to go to d8, and the queen mates on the next move. The engine confirms checkmate in two.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the one queen move that forces checkmate next move.
hints: Black's king is on the edge. Where is a square a knight's jump from it?
From a4, a knight would go to b6 or c5, c3 or b2.
The queen belongs a knight's jump away from the king.
items.explain: Qb6 stands a knight's jump from the king on a4, where the king cannot take her. It leaves the king a single move, Ka3, and the next move is checkmate. The engine confirms mate in two.

items.prompt: White to move. The queen already holds the black king in a small box. Find the one move that forces checkmate next move.
hints: The queen has done her job. Which piece has not helped yet?
Bring your king closer to the black king.
Walk the king toward the black king.
items.explain: Kc6 covers b7, c7 and d7 and the queen holds the b-file, so Black's only move is Kd8. The queen then gives the final check. The engine confirms that Kc6 forces checkmate in two.

items.prompt: You are White with a king and a queen against a lone king. Checkmate within 25 moves. Do not stalemate!

claims.statement: White wins by force from here.

hints: Use the queen to shrink the box. Put her a knight's jump from the king.
Bring your own king close. The final check is usually next to an edge.
Before every move that is not mate, check that Black still has a legal move.
items.explain: King and queen against king is a forced win (the tablebase confirms it from this position). The method: shrink the box with the queen, walk the king up, check on the edge, and never leave Black with no move while not in check.

items.prompt: Black to move. Tap every square the black king can move to.

claims.statement: The black king has exactly these squares.

hints: A rook attacks along its whole rank and file. Which file is this rook on?
The king may not step onto a square the rook attacks.
The three squares on the d-file next to the king are all covered.
items.explain: The rook on d1 attacks the whole d-file, so the king cannot go to d4, d5 or d6. The king is cut off from the left side of the board: it can only use the squares on its own side of the d-file.

items.prompt: White to move. Find checkmate in one.
hints: The two kings face each other with one square between them (e6 and e8). What does the white king cover?
The black king is on the edge. A rook check along the edge would finish it.
Slide the rook to the eighth rank.
items.explain: The white king on e6 covers d7, e7 and f7. The rook checks along the back rank and also covers d8 and f8: checkmate.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the one quiet rook move (no check) that forces checkmate next move.
hints: Black's king is on the eighth rank. Which squares can it use?
The rook can take a whole file away from the king.
A rook on the b-file keeps the king from going to b8.
items.explain: Rb4 takes the b-file away from the black king without giving check. The king is left with one move and the rook then mates on the back rank. The engine confirms checkmate in two.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the one move that forces checkmate next move.
hints: The rook already holds the g-file. Which piece has not helped yet?
Bring the king closer, so it covers the squares the black king would run to.
Move the king one square to the right.
items.explain: Ke6 takes away e7 and f7, and the rook already holds the g-file, so the black king has a single move, Ke8. The rook then mates on the back rank. The engine confirms checkmate in two.

items.prompt: White could also give check at once with Rg8+. Is that a good idea? Predict, then check.
hints: Where is Black's king compared with g8?
Would the rook be protected on g8?
items.explain: The black king stands next to g8 and takes the rook: it is not protected there. A check next to the king only works when your own piece protects the checking piece.

items.prompt: You are White with a king and a rook against a lone king. Checkmate within 40 moves. Keep the rook safe, and do not stalemate!

claims.statement: White wins by force from here.

hints: Use the rook to cut the king off along a file or rank.
Then bring your own king close: it has to help with the final check.
Never leave the rook where the black king can capture it.
items.explain: King and rook against king is a forced win (the tablebase confirms it from this position). It takes longer than with a queen: cut the king off with the rook, walk your king up close to theirs, and check on the edge.
